title: Staged plugin pipeline: CUDA-graph warmup and KV eviction protocol
content:
Purpose
Quick exploration of a staged plugin pipeline that composes TensorRT/Triton-backed execution with occasional custom-kernel fallbacks, plus an explicit CUDA-graph warmup sequence and a KV-cache eviction protocol to reduce noisy cold-starts and reduce tail latency. This is an experimental playbook — not a finalized spec.

Background / motivation
- We observe two main sources of tail latency and non-determinism in current serving: (1) kernel selection and plugin initialization jitter (TensorRT engine loads, Triton model load/fallback) and (2) KV-cache cold misses + high-cost prefill on long-prefix requests.
- Our goal: create a pragmatic runtime pipeline that:
  * favors fast, precompiled execution (TRT engine or preloaded Triton model) when safe
  * transparently falls back to custom kernels for unsupported operators or quantization mismatches
  * uses a short, deterministic CUDA-graph warmup sequence to amortize one-time kernel CUgraph costs
  * introduces a lightweight KV prefetch/eviction protocol that prioritizes prefix reuse for streaming/chat workloads.

Key ideas / components
1) Staged plugin pipeline (runtime flow)
   - Stage 0: fast path — select precompiled TensorRT engine if model variant matches request shape/quantization and operator set fingerprint matches saved fingerprint.
   - Stage 1: Triton-inference path — if TRT engine not available but Triton model instance is warm, route to Triton server (lower startup cost for some graphs).
   - Stage 2: custom-kernel path — for operators or quantization combos not supported by TRT/Triton or when local heuristics flag numerical drift risk. Custom kernels run inside our optimized runtime kernel library.
   - Stage 3: replay / degradation path — if custom kernels fail or OOM, fall back to smaller model variant with explicit response indicating degraded fidelity.
   - Decision heuristics: per-request kernel fingerprinting + short model metadata TTL. Fingerprint = {model-id, seq-len-bucket, quant-mode, enabled-ops-hash}.

2) CUDA-graph warmup protocol
   - Problem: first-time CUDA-graph capture and subsequent kernel JITs introduce tens-to-hundreds ms overhead on some GPUs.
   - Warmup approach: before switching a device into production for a model variant we run a deterministic warmup trace sequence: a) allocate KV cache slices for N prefix lengths (e.g., 8, 64, 256), b) run a synthetic forward with a representative token distribution, c) capture a minimal CUDA graph for the main loop.
   - Warmup constraints: run with limited concurrency (1-2 threads) to avoid interfering with ongoing production serving. Warmup must be cancellable if SLOs are tight.
   - Measurement: record pre/post warmup median latency and 95/99p tail. Only commit TRT engine for routing if warmup improves 95p latency by > 10% vs cold run.

3) KV-cache prefetch and eviction protocol
   - Prefetch idea: For chat/streaming sessions we detect prefix reuse patterns and prefetch KV entries for likely next-token windows during idle CPU cycles. Prefetch runs at lower priority and uses heuristics derived from traffic heatmaps.
   - Eviction policy: hybrid LFU/LRU with sequence-length-aware temperature. Short prefixes (<=32) are cheap; keep them sticky. Long prefixes cost more memory; age them faster.
   - Thresholds: global KV memory cap per GPU; per-session cap set to 3x median session prefix length. Eviction candidates are scored: score = alpha * recency_rank + beta * frequency_rank + gamma * prefix_cost. Tunable defaults: alpha=0.5, beta=0.3, gamma=0.2.
   - Soft-grace eviction: when eviction would impact an in-flight warmup, defer eviction for up to 200ms then proceed. This avoids mid-request eviction thrashing.

4) Scheduling interactions and batching consequences
   - Continuous batching vs deterministic per-request scheduling: kernel staging can interfere with batching if some requests in the batch require different plugin paths. We propose a fast binning policy that groups requests by fingerprint within a short batching window (2–5ms). Batches then route to the common engine; outliers are executed in a focused single-request microbatch to avoid blocking the batch.
   - Batching tradeoff: stricter binning reduces cross-path variance but increases tail latency for outliers. Empirical knob: bin-window size and max-batch-entropy threshold.

Experiment plan (small-scale lab)
A) Baseline runs: 2 model shapes: short-chat (seq=64) and long-instruct (seq=512). Run with three runtime modes: pure TRT (where available), Triton-only, custom-kernel-only. Record median/95/99 latencies, p99.9, GPU memory, and token/sec.
B) Staged pipeline enabled: run same traffic with staged pipeline and with warmup ON/OFF and KV-prefetch ON/OFF. Measure delta compared to baseline.
C) Stress test: bursty arrivals with 90th-percentile concurrency spikes; enable binning window tuning sweep {1,2,5,10}ms.
D) Failure injection: force a TRT engine load failure (simulate file missing or corrupted engine) and observe fallback latency and error rates; measure graceful degradation metrics.

Metrics and success criteria
- p95 improvement >= 15% for short-chat workloads vs Triton-only when warmup + staging is enabled.
- p99 not worse than Triton-only by more than 5% under steady-state load.
- Fallback rate (requests that traverse to custom-kernel path) should be < 5% for tested model variants; if >5%, investigate operator coverage / engine generation problems.
- KV hit-rate improvement by prefetch >= 10% and prefetch cost (additional memory) < 5% of KV budget.

Observed tradeoffs and notes from initial runs (raw lab notes)
- TRT engines gave best throughput but were brittle: minor shape quantization differences created silent engine mismatches that forced fallback. Need stronger fingerprinting metadata embedded at engine build time.
- Triton offered better stability on variable input shapes but introduced a 10–20ms steady overhead per request vs TRT when compared on identical models. Good for mid-sized batches.
- Custom kernels avoid engine load surprises but have higher per-token latency and less optimized fused ops (unless we write fused kernels ourselves). Good fallback but not primary path.
- CUDA-graph warmup reduced the 95p tail significantly on A100/SXM by ~18% for the seq=64 workload, but had diminishing returns for seq=512. Warmup cost was ~120ms per variant per device.
- KV prefetch increased hit-rate by ~12% on chat-like synthetic traces, but naive prefetch caused memory pressure spikes. Implemented soft-prefetch budget helped.

Implementation risks and mitigations
- Risk: engine fingerprint mismatch causing silent correctness regressions. Mitigation: add strict engine-validator harness that runs small unit prompts with golden checksums at engine load time.
- Risk: warmup causing resource contention on busy nodes. Mitigation: global warmup rate limiter and backoff when cluster CPU/gpu utilization > 70%.
- Risk: prefetch overhead spikes memory and evicts hot entries. Mitigation: conservative prefetch budgets, per-device KV watermarks, and prefetch throttling under pressure.

Open questions / TODOs
- How frequently should we regenerate TRT engines vs rely on Triton fallback? (cost/benefit calc for offline engine build infra).
- Explore auto-generated fused custom kernels for the 5 most common op chains to reduce fallback latency.
- Evaluate partial attention offload (attention matmul on custom kernel while rest in TRT) — is cross-plugin boundary state manageable?
- Add deterministic numeric tolerance tests when falling back between engines to capture silent drift.

Immediate next steps (owner: Maya)
- Spin up lab cluster with 2xA100 and run experiment plan A/B. (ETA: 2024-11-16)
- Implement minimal engine fingerprint header in TRT build pipeline and a small validator in the runtime loader. (PR draft: see linked PR)
- Prototype KV soft-prefetcher with adjustable budget and soft-grace eviction in dev branch.

Appendix: quick checklist for experiments
- [ ] baseline runs (TRT/Triton/custom) for seq=64,512
- [ ] staged pipeline + warmup on/off
- [ ] KV-prefetch on/off sweep 
- [ ] batch-window sweep {1,2,5,10}ms
- [ ] failure injection (engine-load, OOM, plugin crash)

Notes-to-self: keep logs verbatim and capture GPU driver versions for each run; small driver differences changed warmup behavior during an earlier test. Also tag experiments with run-id and embed run metadata into artifacts for reproducibility.
